howItWorks.intro: Halloween candy math splits into two problems people constantly mix together: how many pieces you'll actually hand out, and what each of those pieces really costs you. Miscount the first one and you're either dark-porching it by 7:45 or eating stale fun-size Kit Kats in December. Miscount the second and a bag that looked cheap on the shelf ends up costing more than a warehouse variety pack would have. Walk it through with a real street: 65 trick-or-treaters came through a cul-de-sac last year, averaging about 3 pieces each because the bowl was a "take two or three" setup rather than a full-handful free-for-all. Add a 20% buffer for the pack of barely-costumed teenagers who always show up around 8:45, and total pieces needed = 65 × 3 × 1.20 = 234. At $0.15 a piece for a name-brand mix (Reese's, Kit Kat, Twix minis from a Target or Walmart end-cap), candy cost = 234 × $0.15 = $35.10 — about $0.54 per trick-or-treater. A single 105-piece bag doesn't quite cover that, so the actual buy is 3 bags to clear all 234 pieces without a 9 pm gas-station run for backup Skittles.
rules: Total Pieces = Expected Kids x Pieces per Child x (1 + Buffer %)
Candy Cost = Total Pieces x Cost per Piece
Bags Needed = Total Pieces / Pieces per Bag
Cost per Trick-or-Treater = Candy Cost / Expected Kids
howItWorks.outro: These numbers are a starting point, not a promise — actual turnout swings with weather, whether October 31st lands on a weeknight or a Saturday, and whether your street has a reputation as a reliably good candy house. If you've handed out candy at the same address for a few years, your own porch-light tally beats any neighborhood average: jot the headcount in your phone notes each Halloween night and plug last year's real number in next time instead of guessing. First Halloween at a new address? Ask a neighbor who's done it before, or check a local parent Facebook group — many post rough headcounts by zip code every November 1st — and lean toward the higher end of whatever estimate you land on. Running out of candy by 7:30 does more damage to a house's reputation on that street than a modest leftover surplus does to your grocery budget.

faq.question: How much candy do I need for Halloween?
faq.answer: Start with your street type, not a national average. Dense subdivisions and sidewalk-heavy cul-de-sacs often see 80-150 trick-or-treaters over the night; a rural road with houses spaced 200+ feet apart might only see 15-25 total. Apartment or townhome complexes that run a communal trick-or-treat event can spike past 200. Multiply your headcount guess by 2-3 pieces per kid, then add a 15-20% buffer for the second wave of older kids and parents who tend to show up between 8:30 and 9:00 pm, after the youngest trick-or-treaters have already gone home. First year at the address? A neighbor who's handed out candy there before will have a better number than any formula.

faq.question: What is the most cost-effective Halloween candy?
faq.answer: Per-piece cost is the only number that matters, and it swings more than most people expect. Warehouse clubs like Costco, Sam's Club, and BJ's typically run $0.06-$0.09 per piece on 200+ count variety bags of Skittles, Starburst, and M&M's minis. Grocery-store name-brand bags land around $0.12-$0.18 per piece for the same candy in smaller counts. Dollar-store off-brand mixes can dip under $0.05 per piece, but unfamiliar chocolate substitutes often get left in the bowl untouched — a false savings if a third of the bag comes back to you on November 1st. The real move for anyone tracking cost: buy at 50-75% off on November 1st and freeze it for next year. Chocolate holds up fine in the freezer for 8-10 months; gummy candy turns rubbery, so skip that category for stockpiling.

faq.question: When is the best time to buy Halloween candy?
faq.answer: Stores stock Halloween candy heaviest from mid-September through mid-October, and pricing follows a predictable curve. Early-to-mid October is the sweet spot: full selection, and the first round of promo pricing (buy-one-get-one at CVS or Walgreens, per-pound deals at warehouse clubs) has usually kicked in by then. Buy in September and you're paying closer to full retail; wait until October 30-31 and you're picking through whatever's left, usually the flavors nobody wants. If your household tends to raid the bowl before the 31st, buy 5-7 days out instead of three weeks out — a bag of fun-size Twix rarely survives three weeks in a house with kids or a chocolate-loving adult in it.

faq.question: Should I give out full-size bars?
faq.answer: Full-size bars run roughly 7-10x more per piece than fun-size — a full-size Snickers costs about $0.90-$1.10 versus $0.10-$0.15 for the fun-size version — so handing them to all 80+ kids on a busy street can push a $15 candy budget past $80 without much warning. A workable middle ground: reserve full-size bars for the first 20-30 trick-or-treaters, typically the 6:00-7:00 pm window when younger kids come through with parents, then switch to a fun-size bowl once the bigger crowd hits. It also solves a logistics problem — full-size bars run out fast if you don't ration them, and an empty bowl at 7:15 on a night that runs until 9:00 leaves a worse impression than never buying them at all.

faq.question: How much should I budget for Halloween overall, not just candy?
faq.answer: Candy usually makes up 60-70% of a typical household's Halloween spending; decorations and a pumpkin or two cover most of the rest. A household budgeting around $35 for candy on a moderate street should plan another $15-25 for decorations if buying anything beyond what's already boxed up from last year — a couple of pumpkins, string lights, a bag of fake cobwebs. Total spend for a modest but visible setup usually lands between $50 and $90. Skip novelty decorations built for one use only; a $20 inflatable gets reused for years and works out to a few dollars a season, while a $12 bag of yard confetti is gone after one storm.

faq.question: What if I run out of candy before trick-or-treating ends?
faq.answer: Turning off the porch light is the standard signal and nobody takes it personally — a dark porch reads as "no candy here" in most neighborhoods. If you want a backup, keep a $5-10 emergency stash (individually wrapped pretzels, stickers, or a spare small bag bought as insurance) separate from the main bowl, and only open it after 8:30 pm once you can see how the night's turnout compares to your estimate. Running dry is usually a sign to bump next year's buffer from 15% up to 25-30%, especially if Halloween fell on a Friday or Saturday — weekend Halloweens consistently pull 20-40% more trick-or-treaters than weeknight ones because there's no school-night curfew pulling kids home early.
